extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals / PR practitioners who pitch journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting media pitches and press-release style outreach that journalists will open, read, and act on; emphasizes relevance to beat/audience, brevity, timeliness, assets, and exclusivity. Based on a survey of journalists about what makes a pitch publishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant and Tailored to an Audience/Beat
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches must be clearly relevant to the reporter's beat, publication, and audience — personalized beyond just the recipient's name and targeted to their coverage area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists repeatedly said 'relevant' was the most common need (33% of mentions). Personalize to beat, publication, audience, and location; demonstrate you've done homework. Anti-patterns: generic blast pitches, mass outreach, pitching topics outside the reporter's coverage (e.g., pitching California experts to a Wisconsin local). Note: Gmail's new unsubscribe for bulk emails makes irrelevant mass outreach especially risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise / Gets to the Point Quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches should be brief and skimmable — get to the point immediately and keep body length short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many journalists prefer ~25 words or fewer, 3–5 sentences, or 1–2 short paragraphs; bullets improve skimmability. Industry variation exists (fashion/retail value brevity most). Anything much longer risks violating journalists' 'concise' rule. Include necessary who/what/when/why succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localized or Contains a Local Angle
rubrics_metrics.description: For local or community outlets, pitches should include a defined geographic/locational hook and local sources or interviewees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over 200 responses emphasized locality: local tie-ins, regional sources, and a clear explanation of why the story matters to that community. Anti-patterns: sending national/regional pitches without local relevance; labeling a huge area as 'local'. Providing ready access to local sources and interviewees increases chances of pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and Newsworthy (Strong 'Why Now')
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches must offer a genuine news angle or timely 'news peg' that explains why the story matters now, not just product promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists look for new, trending angles and a compelling 'why now' beyond self-promotion. For breaking news or studies, provide rapid access to sources/data and explain the relevance to current events or trends. Example guidance: pitch immediately after a study with an expert available for a quick interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offers Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering exclusivity — either exclusive access to sources/data or pitching a single reporter — is appealing and can increase pick-up odds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters value being the first or sole outlet with a scoop; exclusivity must be stated clearly. Important nuance: exclusivity is about pitching a single person (not emailing multiple people at one outlet). Anti-pattern: emailing several reporters at the same company on the same day, which often ruins chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provides Helpful Assets (Quotes, Images, Video, Data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include relevant, high-quality assets such as quotes, high-resolution images, video links, infographics, and data to add context and save reporters' time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assets should be directly useful and relevant; include permissions/credits and links to downloads. Examples: large feature-ready photo for WordPress, data files, ready quotes, video links. Anti-patterns: low-quality or irrelevant assets; failing to provide usage permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contains Compelling Storytelling and Unique Angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond facts, successful pitches frame a compelling narrative with fresh, journalistically interesting angles rather than overt marketing messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists rewarded pitches that offered new/unreported aspects, clear hooks, and transparent, authentic presentation without excessive hype/jargon. A strong pitch combines relevance, clarity, and storytelling and may include a call to action or next steps to convert interest into coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear Subject Line / Direct Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a concise, descriptive subject line that functions like a headline and entices the reporter to open the email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists recommended direct headlines and brief descriptive subject lines — some suggest a 25-word tease in the subject to entice reading. Subject lines should summarize the pitch's news/value and align with the body copy for quick triage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting: Plain Text Body; Avoid PDFs
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver the pitch as plain text in the email body and avoid attachments like PDFs that impede quick reading or copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters noted that PDFs cause formatting issues when copying/pasting; plain text with bullets is preferred for skimmability. Use inline bullets or short paragraphs rather than heavy formatting or attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect Journalists' Time / Provide Clear CTA and Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of reporters' time by making next steps obvious (call to action), including who to contact, interview availability, and providing rapid follow-up options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear who/what/when/why and state if experts are available for quick interviews (example: live three-minute interview for a breaking study). Respectful practice: be transparent about sponsorship asks, avoid requiring excessive hoops, and make it easy to act on the pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Mass Outreach / Don't Blanket-pitch Same Outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not send the same pitch to many reporters at once, and avoid blanket pitching large lists; tailored, targeted outreach is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists dislike receiving identical pitches across colleagues; offices discuss pitches and identical ones are often rejected. Gmail's bulk-email handling (Unsubscribe) further penalizes mass sends. Antipatterns: emailing thousands or 5k+ recipients or multiple people at the same media company the same day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide Relevant Permissions and Rights for Content
rubrics_metrics.description: If offering images, content, or coverage-ready materials, clarify usage rights, credits, and exclusivity terms upfront.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists appreciated pitches that included 'exclusive rights to run the content' or clarified permissions/credits. Make clear whether images are feature-ready, who to credit, and whether the outlet has rights to reuse assets.
